Have you profiled any real code with this change? Looking at your results, the performance improvements seem mixed in the benchmarks from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106996. But ultimately, arbitrary benchmarks are not good indicators of whether a given data structure will perform well with real world data. The only way of knowing whether they will perform well with real world data is to test with real world data. 

AHashMap is used in a number of performance sensitive areas in the engine. I suggest picking one of them and profiling a real world situation where performance is limited by the speed of the hash map and then see how this PR compares to the current implementation in practice.

But ultimately, arbitrary benchmarks are not good indicators of whether a given data structure will perform well with real world data. The only way of knowing whether they will perform well with real world data is to test with real world data.
> 
> AHashMap is used in a number of performance sensitive areas in the engine. I suggest picking one of them and profiling a real world situation where performance is limited by the speed of the hash map and then see how this PR compares to the current implementation in practice.

I do agree with your perspective, and I am trying to find more practical examples, yet their results are about the same as the current one's. Benchmarks on the [godot/godot_benchmarks](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-benchmarks) yield about a 5% difference on navigation and animation tests, and the animation test on the #92554 had only one FPS of difference (72 to 73), which are almost insignificant.

Also, because this PR is about a major architectural change on a core data structure, there is also a risk of regressions in some cases as well. The current implementation and my implementation have different bad-cases, and these differences may cause some headaches if not tested enough.

Another thing I want to say is that, as now I broke out of the cycle of code-test-bench-repeat, I am looking at this from another perspective, and I think, even if implemented perfectly, the mentioned optimizations above may not make a big difference. I am saying this as AHashMap, currently, has slightly different goals than SwissTable. AHashMap, while a hashmap with fast insertion and lookup times, somewhat prioritizes iteration speed, thus makes use of a dense array to store its values. Swisstable also uses an array to store its values but it scatters them around just like its metadata, thus slower iteration compared to AHashMap. For this reason, AHashMap has to store a position value mapped to its metadata, while SwissTable has no such restriction. If we want to make use of SwissTable's advantages to the fullest, we may need to add another hashmap implementation.

Hi! We are aware of swiss tables, and have considered their introduction into the codebase. It's a great hashing container, and (as far as I've seen), suitable for a 'general purpose' hash table.
Note that a similar change has been already been proposed (WIP https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/101133).

That being said, your current implementation has two major problems that are not present in either `AHashMap` or abseil's `flat_hash_map`:
- It uses an additional positions array, requiring more RAM.
- Due to the positions indirection, it has a new cache miss on cold access.

While, as you've found, hot access can be quite a lot faster than `AHashMap`, _cold_ access is often more important. Cache misses are likely to be more expensive than the actual hashing iteration[^1]. This is unfortunately also pretty cumbersome to test, so my tests from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106996 did not cover cold access (instead, I reasoned about it).
Likewise, the additional use of RAM is a hard sell, and cannot be regarded as a 'pure' improvement over `AHashMap`.

Both problems, especially taken together, make the change unacceptable as a patch to `AHashMap`.
Considering this, swiss tables would need to be a _new_ type instead (e.g. `SwissHashMap`). Looking at your latest comment, I see you have reached a similar conclusion.

However, introducing a new map type comes with its own problems. For example, we [already have](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12515) ~4 of them. In addition, `AHashMap` is already a pretty capable hash map. We are not in any rush to replace it. 

Adding a new hashing table would require you to show measurable benefit in existing code (as @clayjohn mentioned). 5% improvement in navigation is nice, but it's not something we'd be willing to introduce a new hash map implementation over right now. 
I have no doubt we'll find a use case for swiss tables sooner or later, given their excellent lookup speed. But again, we're not in any rush for it. Practically, most currently bottlenecked code is using `HashMap`, which would already be quite a lot better with `AHashMap`.

So, to summarize: 
- This is a great idea! 
- This needs to be its own hash map type, rather than a change to `AHashMap`.
- We need to find a practical use-case to add it, where it provides tangible benefit over `AHashMap`.

[^1]: Loosely oriented by Agner Fog's guidelines, especially the associated cycle costs of cold RAM lookup https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

Hi! I was away for sometime due to my senior thesis and other personal stuff, actually, I am still away from my home and unable to do any heavy programming tasks.

I have seen #101133 before and had benchmarked against it as well, but I don't have the data right now due to the reason I have mentioned above. The reason I made a seperate PR was that the code there was too complex, wasn't updated for while (I was not able to even compile it without merging it with the current master), and I actually started working on it before I saw it. And even though my implementation was much more simpler, it was able to compete with it and was also crushing on insertion times, at least on the benchmarks.

On the topic of hot access, I agree with you. Cold access is hard to emulate and there doesn't seem to be many tools to help with it. I tried that on my benchmarks, but to no avail.

A minor point I want to mention is that, Rust's [indexmap](https://github.com/indexmap-rs/indexmap) and [ordermap](https://github.com/indexmap-rs/ordermap) also has a similar API and features to AHashMap and uses a SwissTable impl. under the hood. It might be worthwhile to take a look at them in the future.

Another point, I want to mention is that, during the time I was away, I did some more research on SwissTable, and... it seems that my implementation is not really a SwissTable. It was just another open address hashtable, with the difference of using only one byte per metadata. My implementation did not employ a grouping mechanism. The thing that made me realize this fact was [a post on Go Blog](https://go.dev/blog/swisstable). For this reason **I will convert this PR to a draft**, in case I work on it to make it a proper one later.

For my last point, which may be a bit offtopic, looking at the [proposal mentioned](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12515), HashSet might actually be a good testing ground for a SwissTable-like implementation. I will be away from home for about 2 months, so I am unable to work on it myself for the time being.
